stated_availability: No dedicated data-availability statement appears in the article (the end matter runs: CRediT authorship contribution statement -> "Declaration of competing interest / None" -> Acknowledgements -> "Appendix A. Supplementary data" -> References). The only availability statements are: (1) "Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921." (Appendix A, p. 18); (2) "All analyses were undertaken in 'R' version 4.3.0. The script to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information." (s2.3.3, p. 4); (3) "The script used to run all case study tests is available in the supplementary information." (s2.4, p. 4). Underlying morphometric data are pointed to via in-article summary tables (Tables 1, 5-7) and via citation to prior publications, theses, and monographs; no repository deposit, dataset DOI, or accession is stated anywhere. Article is open access under CC BY 4.0. DESCRIPTIVE ONLY - not mapped to L1-L6 (L-levels are assigned at reproduction time per preregistration s7.3).

F1.evidence: No dataset-level persistent identifier of any kind. The only PID in the paper is the article DOI ("https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921", title page and Appendix A), which identifies the journal article, not the data. No Zenodo/figshare/Dryad DOI, no tDAR or Open Context identifier, no accession number, no IGSN for the physical replica or excavated assemblages (the replica points are said to be "curated in the Kent State University Experimental Archaeology Laboratory" with no sample identifiers). Per pid-systems-guide, a dataset PID (DOI, accession, or repository-specific) is absent.

F2.evidence: No structured metadata record exists for any dataset: there is no repository landing page, README, data dictionary, or DataCite/JSON-LD record. Data are described only in narrative prose and in-article summary tables (e.g. Table 1 gives only "Mean, SD, CV, Minimum, Maximum" for the two replica assemblages). The structured metadata that does exist (authors, title, keywords "Morphometrics; Incomplete record; Fragmentary data; Archaeological discovery; Lithics; Ceramics; Metals", abstract) describes the article, not a data resource. Scored 0 per fair-principles-guide F2 ("Repository provides structured metadata ... -> 1 point").

F3.evidence: Unscoreable and therefore 0: with no data identifier assigned (F1 = 0) there is no identifier for metadata to include. No metadata record explicitly carries a dataset DOI or accession; the DOI cited in Appendix A ("Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921.") is the article identifier.

F4.evidence: The data are not registered or indexed in any searchable data registry. No deposit in Zenodo, figshare, Dryad, DataCite, tDAR, Open Context, or ARIADNEplus is mentioned. The only indexing is of the journal article itself on ScienceDirect/Crossref, which is a literature index, not a data registry.

A1.evidence: A1 completeness rule applied: data_completeness.coverage_category = "minimal" (0/13 datasets at Tier 0-2), so A1 = 0. The bulk of the research data is co-author held or locked in unpublished theses and paywalled monographs (e.g. "Martin-Ramos, C., 2022. ... Unpublished PhD thesis. University College London."; "Key, A.J.M., 2015. Form and Function in the Lower Palaeolithic. Unpublished PhD Thesis. University of Kent."), and the article shares only summary statistics (Tables 1, 5-7). No ethical/legal restriction is claimed anywhere, so the CARE/ethics exception does not apply.

A1_1.evidence: For the accessible portion (supplementary tables/figures and the in-article tables), retrieval is by plain HTTPS from an open-access article: "Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921." and "This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)". Protocol is open, free, universally implementable, and requires no login or paid subscription.

A1_2.evidence: Assessed for the accessible portion per fair-principles-guide ("Evaluates protocol quality for the accessible portion of the data"): delivery is over HTTPS/DOI resolution, which supports authentication and authorisation where necessary, and no restriction is needed because the article and its supplement are openly licensed CC BY 4.0. Noted caveat: the inaccessible majority of the data has no documented access procedure at all (no "available on request" clause, no ethical justification), which is a negative signal but falls outside the accessible-portion framing of this sub-principle.

A2.evidence: The descriptive metadata for the data (Table 1 descriptive statistics; Tables 5-7 with n, means, minima, maxima per variable; the per-case-study Methods descriptions) reside in a DOI-registered, Crossref-indexed, open-access journal article ("Journal of Archaeological Science 162 (2024) 105921"; "https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921") under publisher preservation. This metadata persists independently of, and would survive the loss of, any supplementary data file.

I1.evidence: The data as shared are unstructured for machine use: the substantive figures are printed tables inside a PDF (Tables 1-7) plus supplementary tables/figures whose formats are never stated. No machine-actionable format (CSV with schema, JSON, XML, GeoPackage) is declared anywhere. Per fair-principles-guide: "Data in PDF supplementary materials is available but not machine-actionable"; "Unstructured format (PDF tables, Word doc, ...) -> 0 points".

I2.evidence: No controlled vocabularies or ontologies are used or cited. Artefact typologies ("Thebes cluster" style, Clovis/Folsom/Midland, "Impressed Ware" and "Stentinello" styles) and chronological terms (MIS 15, Howiesons Poort, Middle Historic) are free-text with bibliographic citations only; no PeriodO, Getty AAT, Pleiades, CIDOC-CRM, or ARIADNEplus URIs. Keywords are uncontrolled free text.

I3.evidence: Links to upstream data sources are bibliographic, not PID-based. Relationships are stated in prose (e.g. "Data are derived from Buchanan and Hamilton's (2021) study of scaling laws in Paleoindian points"; "The methods used to collect these data have been previously described in Martin-Ramos (2022).") but resolve only to author-date entries in the reference list, most of which carry no DOI. No typed, machine-actionable references ("isDerivedFrom [DOI]") to datasets, samples, or software.

R1.evidence: Rich human-readable documentation of the data is present (fair-principles-guide: "Detailed documentation, README, data dictionary, methods description? -> 1 point"). Each dataset is described with sample size, variables, units, site, chronology, and selection criteria - e.g. "we limit the present case study to the whole flakes excavated from MIS 15 sediments in the 2020 season (n = 173)"; Table 1 reports Mean/SD/CV/Minimum/Maximum for length, breadth, thickness, mass, elongation, refinement, PC1 and PC2; Tables 5-7 give per-variable n, mean, min and max for every case study; exclusion rules are stated (microliths lacking thickness measures excluded; "two outliers have been removed from the assemblage of phase B after the performance of exploratory principal component analyses (PCAs)").

R1_1.evidence: A clear, accessible, machine-readable licence with URI covers the article and its supplementary material: "0305-4403/(c) 2023 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)" (title page). Maps to SPDX CC-BY-4.0. Caveat: no separate data-specific licence is stated.

R1_2.evidence: Detailed provenance is documented for the datasets: creation process ("500 replica Acheulean handaxes were produced by Key and Lycett (2017) on British flint over the course of 18 months"; the replica points "were originally knapped by M.I.E. in 2021" and "the specimens have since been curated in the Kent State University Experimental Archaeology Laboratory"), instruments ("which were measured using diameter boards with 1 cm increments, callipers and a metal rule (see: Petrie, 2020)"; "The metric data were recorded in centimetres from plan-view and profile-view digital images."), upstream sources cited per case study, and funding for data collection itemised in the Acknowledgements (British Academy Fellowship, Leakey Foundation Grants, "London NERC DTP training grant NE/L002485/1").

R1_3.evidence: No domain-relevant community data standard is applied: no Dublin Core/DataCite metadata, no ARIADNEplus, CIDOC-CRM, or Darwin Core encoding, and no deposit in a domain repository (tDAR, Open Context, ADS). Measurement protocols follow published conventions (e.g. "following the method outlined by de la Pena and Wadley (2014)"; "recorded in mm following Buchanan and Hamilton (2021)"), but that is methodological convention rather than a data/metadata community standard.

F1.evidence: No software persistent identifier. The scripts are located only by prose pointers to the supplement ("The script to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information."; "The script used to run all case study tests is available in the supplementary information.") which resolve via the article DOI "https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921". No Zenodo software DOI, no SWHID, no CRAN package, no GitHub release - despite the title advertising "Method validation, case studies, and code".

F2.evidence: No structured software metadata: no CodeMeta.json, no CITATION.cff, no software name, version, or dependency declaration. The code is described in two sentences of running text plus the runtime version ("All analyses were undertaken in 'R' version 4.3.0."). No repository record supplies authors/title/description for the software artefact.

F3.evidence: Unscoreable and therefore 0: no software identifier is assigned (F1 = 0), so no metadata record can explicitly include one. The only identifier printed is the article DOI.

F4.evidence: The code is not registered or indexed in any software registry: not on CRAN, Zenodo, Software Heritage, JOSS, or GitHub. It exists solely as publisher-hosted supplementary files attached to the article record.

A1.evidence: The code is stated to be retrievable in full via a standard protocol: "The script to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information." (s2.3.3) and "The script used to run all case study tests is available in the supplementary information." (s2.4), reachable by HTTPS/DOI resolution per "Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921." The two statements together cover both analytical components of the paper (validation tests and case studies). The data-completeness rule in the instrument constrains data A1 only; it is not applied to code.

A1_1.evidence: Retrieval is by open, free, universally implementable HTTPS from an open-access article - "This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)" - with no login, subscription, or proprietary client required.

A1_2.evidence: Delivery over HTTPS/DOI resolution supports authentication and authorisation where necessary; no access restriction is imposed or needed on the scripts, which are openly published with the CC BY article. No closed or gated component of the code is described.

A2.evidence: The record documenting the code - its existence, purpose, and runtime environment ("All analyses were undertaken in 'R' version 4.3.0.") - sits in a DOI-registered, Crossref-indexed, publisher-preserved open-access article (Journal of Archaeological Science 162 (2024) 105921). That metadata persists independently of the supplementary script files themselves.

I1.evidence: The code uses a formal, open, broadly implemented language with the version pinned: "All analyses were undertaken in 'R' version 4.3.0." Plain R source in a standard, non-proprietary representation; matches fair-principles-guide I1 for software ("standard format - Python/R code").

I2.evidence: No vocabulary or metadata standard for software is used - no CodeMeta terms, no SPDX identifier declaration in the artefact, no ontology-based description of the analysis. Ad hoc description only.

I3.evidence: No qualified, PID-based references from the code to other resources. R package dependencies are never listed; the OLE implementation's antecedents are cited only bibliographically ("The formulaic expression of OLE is widely available through open-access sources (e.g., Pimiento and Clements, 2014; Roberts et al., 2021; Key et al., 2021b)"), with no DOIs or typed relationships attached to the scripts.

R1.evidence: A detailed methods description of what the code implements is present (fair-principles-guide R1 accepts "methods description"): R 4.3.0; k values of 5, 10, 20 and 30 ("we also assessed the use of k values of 5, 20 and 30 for all validation tests"); random subsampling "at rates of 5%, 10%, 20%, and 50% relative to the total number of records"; "One thousand iterations of each process were performed for all subsampling percentages and k"; the duplicate-handling routine ("we resampled each value from a normal distribution, where we used the value itself as the mean, and a very small standard deviation (0.001). We repeated the OLE procedure with randomised values for 1000 iterations"); and the 95% CI (T_CI) coverage criterion. Caveat: no README, usage instructions, or dependency list accompanies the artefact.

R1_1.evidence: The scripts are released under the article's clear, accessible licence: "This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)" (SPDX CC-BY-4.0). Caveat: CC BY is a content licence, not a software licence, and no code-specific LICENCE file or SPDX declaration is provided.

R1_2.evidence: The software artefact carries no detailed provenance: no code authorship is attributed anywhere - the CRediT statement assigns no "Software" role to any of the eleven authors (e.g. "Alastair Key: Conceptualization, Data curation, Formal analysis, Investigation, Methodology, Validation, Writing - original draft, Writing - review & editing."; "Ivan Jaric: Formal analysis, Methodology, Resources, Writing - original draft, Writing - review & editing."), despite Software being CRediT role 9. No script version, no version control or commit history, no dependency provenance, and no derivation record for the code beyond the runtime version statement.

R1_3.evidence: No research-software community standards are met: no archival deposit with PID, no CITATION.cff or CodeMeta, no dependency management (renv.lock/DESCRIPTION), no containerisation, no tests, no installation instructions. On the fair-principles-guide computational reproducibility spectrum this sits at Level 1 ("Code only ... no dependency specification, no environment documentation").

barriers: No data availability statement in the article; only R scripts and results tables/figures are stated to be in the supplement, never the underlying morphometric records

Co-author gatekeeping: ten of the thirteen datasets were contributed by co-authors credited only with the CRediT 'Resources' role (Bebber, Buchanan, Cortell-Nicolau, Martin-Ramos, de la Pena, Petrie, Proffitt, Robb, Michelaki), with no deposit or access route given

Unpublished theses: Olduvai Bed III-IV cleavers cite 'Martin-Ramos, C., 2022. ... Unpublished PhD thesis. University College London.'; the eight supplementary Acheulean assemblages cite 'Key, A.J.M., 2015. Form and Function in the Lower Palaeolithic. Unpublished PhD Thesis. University of Kent.'
Closed monographs/paywall: Bannu Basin bowls (n approx. 1466) derive from Petrie (2020), Oxbow Books; Neolithic Impressed Ware and Stentinello pots from Robb (2007), Cambridge University Press

Summary statistics only: the article shares Mean/SD/CV/Minimum/Maximum (Table 1) and mean/min/max per variable (Tables 5-7), which are insufficient to re-run OLE - the model requires the k largest or smallest individual records

Upstream datasets cited by author-date only (Key and Lycett 2017; Key et al. 2022; de la Pena and Wadley 2014; Buchanan and Hamilton 2021; Cortell-Nicolau et al. 2023; Proffitt et al. 2016) with methods, not data, stated as available there

Enumeration follows the paper's own units: 2 replica validation assemblages (handaxes n=500; Early Archaic points n=45) + the 'Ten case studies ... investigated here' (Old Park flakes n=173; Boxgrove handaxes n=254; Olduvai cleavers n=134; Sibudu bipolar cores n=131; Paleoindian points n=1281 across four types; geometric microliths n=734 across phases A and B; capuchin flakes n=31; copper socketed tang points n=93; Middle Historic bowls n up to 1466; Neolithic Impressed Ware and Stentinello pots) + 1 supplementary comparison set (eight Acheulean assemblages from Key 2015, Fig. 6C) = 13; all classified Tier 3 (exists but inaccessible), none Tier 0-2. No ethically restricted data is claimed, so the CARE exception does not offset the shortfall.
